OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the imaging modalities used to diagnose and manage musculoskeletal tumors.
Perform an appropriate imaging-based workup and evaluation for patients with
musculoskeletal tumors.
Identify lesions as aggressive or nonaggressive based on imaging features.
Determine the evolving role of MRI and positron emission tomography in orthopaedic
oncology.
Generate an appropriate surveillance strategy for musculoskeletal oncology patients.
Introduction
Although primary bone and soft-tissue tumors are relatively uncommon, appropriate imaging
studies are essential if tumors are suspected or incidentally detected. The clinical presentation

Radiographs are the most appropriate initial imaging study for screening and characterization
of bone lesions. Radiographs may provide sufficient information for diagnosis and to guide the
treating clinician; however, even if conventional radiographs alone are inadequate, they often
guide the selection of the most appropriate next step for advanced imaging studies.

CT provides complementary information, with its ability to detect subtle matrix mineralization
or periosteal reaction that may not be observed on radiographs.
MRI typically is the most appropriate next step for soft-tissue tumors, allowing for evaluation
of the tissue composition (eg, fat, hemorrhage, fluid levels) and anatomic extent.
Advances in MRI, CT, and nuclear medicine have improved the ability of surgeons to define
lesions on diagnosis, assess response to therapy, and conduct surveillance with increased
accuracy and lower radiation exposure.2
The use of positron emission tomography (PET) in the evaluation and assessment of bone and
soft-tissue tumors continues to increase and evolve.
Radiography
Although some tumors can be diagnosed with certainty based on their radiographic
appearance, more often, the information provided by radiographs allows for a differential
diagnosis to be formulated.

Matrix of the lesion
Rings/stipples suggest chondroid matrix.
Cloudlike suggests bone formation/osteoblastic.
Nature and extent of soft-tissue involvement
The collective radiographic characteristics should be used to classify the lesion as
aggressive (potentially malignant) or nonaggressive (most benign; Figure 7)
Nonaggressive characteristics include a narrow zone of transition, an intact cortex, smooth
periosteal reaction, and lack of an associated soft-tissue mass.3,4
Aggressive characteristics include a wide zone of transition between the tumor and the
surrounding normal bone, cortical destruction, interrupted periosteal reaction, and an
associated soft-tissue mass.3,5-7

Hemangiomas: phleboliths in soft tissue

Computed Tomography
Except in certain circumstances, CT is not routinely used for the evaluation of bone and soft-
tissue lesions.
Myositis ossificans8 (Figure 10)
Osteoid osteoma (Figure 11)
To delineate a bone tumor in a complex anatomic location, such as the pelvis or scapula
In patients who cannot undergo MRI because of an MRI-incompatible device
CT routinely is used for staging of suspected malignancies.
Chest CT for patients with bone and soft-tissue sarcomas at risk of pulmonary metastases
Chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT for patients with metastatic lesions with unknown primary
site

Figure 10 Images of the elbow of a 25-year-old man with an elbow mass. A, Lateral radiograph
demonstrates periosteal calcification along the anterior margin of the proximal radius. B, Sagittal
contrast-enhanced, T1-weighted, fat-suppressed MRI shows the hypervascular soft-tissue mass
and bone marrow edema within the proximal radius (not shown). C, Sagittal reformatted image
from an axial CT scan obtained 4 weeks after the radiograph shown in panel A reveals
characteristic peripheral calcification extending from the periosteum, which is characteristic of
myositis ossificans. This lesion has a typically aggressive, masslike appearance on MRI. High-

concern. (Reproduced from Ecklund K: Imaging of musculoskeletal tumors: Updates and current

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the preferred advanced three-dimensional imaging modality for most bone and soft-
tissue neoplasms.
For osseous lesions, MRI is highly accurate in delineating bone marrow involvement,
intraosseous extent, skip metastases, and soft-tissue extension10 (Figure 12).

Figure 12 MRIs of a left anterior thigh with a soft-tissue mass. T2-weighted axial (A); T1-
weighted axial (B); T1-weighted, fat-saturated axial (C); and T1-weighted, fat-saturated,
contrast-enhanced axial (D) MRIs show the mass in the quadriceps musculature. Fat signal is
observed on all pulse sequences (solid arrows). No intrinsic or perilesional edema or
enhancement is observed. These imaging findings are diagnostic of a nonaggressive
intramuscular lipoma. T1-weighted axial (E), T2-weighted axial (F), and coronal short tau
inversion recovery (G) MRIs show the mass in the quadriceps musculature, abutting the femur.
An isohyperintense signal is observed on the T1-weighted MRI (solid arrow) and a
heterogeneous hyperintense signal is observed on the T2-weighted and short tau inversion
recovery MRIs (solid arrows). The size (more than 19 cm in the greatest dimension), deep
location, and heterogeneous signal characteristics are concerning for an aggressive malignant
lesion. The mass was subsequently resected and was diagnosed as a dedifferentiated
liposarcoma. (Reproduced from Cordle AC, Andres CL: Evaluation of soft-tissue tumors in
Bierman JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 15-24.)
For soft-tissue tumors, MRI provides unparalleled anatomic detail.
Invasion/encroachment of nearby neurovascular structures
Demarcation of normal from abnormal tissue
Visualization of tissue planes surrounding a lesion
Specifics regarding standard and advanced MRI sequences are beyond the scope of this
lesson; however, some general guidelines are specific to tumors.

MRI to evaluate musculoskeletal tumors should include intravenous contrast.
Differentiation between cystic and solid masses
Evaluation of hematomas
Identification of areas for biopsy
Most bone and soft-tissue tumors have low or intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted
MRIs and high signal intensity on T2-weighted MRIs.
Certain lesions can be determined definitively via analysis of MRIs (eg, lipomatous lesions,
cysts, hemangiomas). These can be managed definitively without biopsy10 (Figure 13). 
Figure 13 Images of the left knee of a 12-year-old boy with activity-related medial knee pain. A,
AP radiograph demonstrates a radiolucent, geographic lesion involving the medial metaphysis.
B, T1-weighted axial MRI shows a well-demarcated lesion with multiple fluid-fluid levels. C, T1-
weighted coronal, fat-suppressed pre-contrast MRI shows chronic cortical expansion with
associated marrow and soft-tissue edema. D, Coronal contrast-enhanced MRI shows a varying
degree of enhancement compared with the pre-contrast MRI shown in panel C. Biopsy
revealed an aneurysmal bone cyst. (Reproduced from Cummings JE: Evaluation of bone
tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors,
ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 3-14.)
Certain MRI findings are suggestive of aggressiveness and potential malignancy.11,12
Size larger than 5 cm
Location deep to the fascia
Heterogeneous signal intensity
Ill-defined margins
Invasion of adjacent structures
Perilesional edema
Intralesional necrosis and hemorrhage

Heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement
According to a retrospective review of 266 masses, the combination of signal intensity, size,
and depth resulted in a sensitivity of 64%, a specificity of 85%, and an accuracy of 77% for
the differentiation of benign soft-tissue lesions from malignant soft-tissue lesions.13
If the nature of the lesion cannot be determined via analysis of MRIs, then biopsy may be
required before definitive management.
Bone Scintigraphy
Useful as a screening tool to assess for multiple sites of bone involvement or skip metastases
Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy
Technetium-99m forms chemical adducts to sites of new bone formation.
Very sensitive but not specific
High false-negative rate in multiple myeloma and in very osteolytic bone metastasis, such as
renal cell carcinoma
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography may be used as an initial imaging modality for the evaluation of soft-tissue
masses.
Advantages include low cost, availability, and lack of ionizing radiation.
Disadvantages include limitations in tissue characterization and dependency on the skill level
of the operator.
Can accurately characterize location, size, echogenicity, margins, vascularity, solid versus
cystic, and compressibility
High sensitivity but low specificity14
Reported diagnostic accuracies for assessment of soft-tissue masses range from 77% to
93%.15,16
Positron Emission Tomography
The use of fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET and indication guidelines are evolving.
The standardized update value (SUV) provides a quantitative measure of metabolic activity.
Malignant tumors generally have a higher SUV compared with that of benign tumors.
The use of SUV values for diagnosis and assessment continues to expand.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004038
16/22

For example, in a study, the sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy of FDG PET/CT
in differentiating malignant pathologic fractures from benign pathologic fractures were
89.5%, 86.7%, and 88.2%, respectively, with a cut-off maximum SUV set at 4.7.17
The combined information provided by FDG PET/CT offers excellent sensitivity for initial
staging and good sensitivity for assessment of recurrence of soft-tissue and bone sarcomas.18
Ability to evaluate osseous and non-osseous sites, including the lymphatic system
In bone sarcomas
PET/CT is replacing bone scintigraphy for initial staging.
FDG PET may substitute for bone marrow biopsy in Ewing sarcoma.19
FDG PET has a role in assessing the response to chemotherapy20-22 (Figure 14).
Figure 14 Positron emission tomography/CT scans of the right scapula of a 21-year-old man
with Ewing sarcoma. A, Image obtained before neoadjuvant chemotherapy shows an
expansile, ill-defined, destructive lytic/soft--tissue lesion in the medial scapula, with a
maximum standardized uptake value of 7.2. B, Image obtained after neoadjuvant
chemotherapy shows substantial interval decrease in metabolic activity(standardized uptake
value of 2.6). (Courtesy of David D. Greenberg, MD, St. Louis, MO.)
In soft-tissue sarcomas
PET shows promise in differentiating benign and malignant peripheral nerve sheath
tumors23,24
The appropriate role of PET/CT in soft-tissue sarcomas, especially those with a propensity
for lymphatic spread, currently is undefined.
PET/CT continues to increase in popularity for staging and surveillance of metastatic
carcinoma, multiple myeloma, and lymphoma.

A recent study found that PET/CT may not provide any additional benefit over the standard
evaluation for identification of primary cancer in patients with a skeletal metastasis of
unknown origin; however, it may be an effective screening tool, equivalent or superior to the
standard diagnostic algorithm for evaluation of the overall metastatic burden in these
patients.25
Surveillance
Surveillance to detect local or distant recurrence, identify adverse effects of management, and
extend disease-free survival is an important component of oncology.
The specific imaging modalities depend on the location of the primary tumor and the sites of
metastatic spread.
Radiographs for local recurrence after primary bone tumor resection
MRI with contrast for local recurrence after resection of soft-tissue tumor
Chest imaging for bone and soft-tissue sarcomas given their propensity for pulmonary
metastases
The duration of surveillance needs to continue throughout the period of time in which the
tumor is likely to recur.
Sarcoma surveillance strategies have wide variation without high-quality evidence supporting
the different protocols.26
Surveillance may be performed in accordance with the National Comprehensive Cancer
Network guidelines.
The National Comprehensive Cancer Network sarcoma follow-up guidelines call for chest
radiographs or chest CT scans every 3 to 6 months for 2 to 3 years, every 6 months for the
next 2 years, and then annually.27
A randomized noninferiority trial demonstrated that chest radiography did not lead to
poorer survival and was not inferior to chest CT in terms of detecting pulmonary
metastasis during sarcoma surveillance.28
Different modalities for surveillance imaging for distant metastases, such as PET/CT and
whole-body MRI, are in clinical use.
Each are associated with advantages and disadvantages.
Factors to consider include sensitivity of modality, cost, and irradiation for the patient.
Guidelines are updated as evidence becomes available.

Summary
Imaging continues to play an important role in the diagnosis and management of
musculoskeletal tumors.
Radiography remains an important initial imaging modality for most lesions.
Many imaging modalities are available, and new technologies are being discovered.
The role of ultrasonography, CT, MRI, and PET/nuclear medicine varies based on the tumor.
Guidelines exist to aid in diagnosis of the condition and monitor the patient.
Emphasis on reduction of irradiation and evidence-based practice should be the basis for
updating these guidelines moving forward.
